whyText: Partner’s family is in Munich; I want to hold my own at dinner.
experienceText: Two Duolingo streaks that died; I can order food.

approach.approachNotes: You'll get the most from comprehensible input paired with real output: hear or read German at your level, then produce your own sentences, not just recognize them. Since Munich dinners are the goal, build around spoken, social register — greetings, family talk, food, opinions — over textbook grammar drills. Until we know your level, early sessions will test where you land; if you already know some German, we'll skip basics and go straight to gaps. As you progress, scaffolding (translations, sentence starters) fades and improvisation load increases.
pitfalls: Recognizing words when reading feels like fluency but doesn't mean you can produce them aloud.
Overusing English grammar logic causes systematic errors in case endings and word order.
Politeness and small talk phrases get neglected in favor of vocabulary lists, hurting real dinners.
progressionPrinciples: Start with high-frequency social phrases and questions before tackling grammar rules abstractly.
Interleave listening and speaking early so output habits form alongside comprehension.
Sequence topics around real family-dinner scenarios: introductions, food, opinions, small talk.

successOutcomes: I can follow a dinner conversation
I can tell a short story about my week
I feel relaxed speaking with family
